title: How to Care for a Dying Loved One
excerpt: Walking someone toward death is among the holiest and hardest things a person can do. It will cost you more than you have, and it is worth all of it.
body:
Few things ask more of us than caring for someone we love as they die. It is long, it is exhausting, it is full of impossible decisions and small indignities and a grief that begins before the death does. And it is holy ground. To accompany a person through the last door is to do something the world mostly hides and looks away from, and to do it well is one of the deepest acts of love there is. If you are in it now, or about to be, here is what I have learned from the bedsides.

## Be present more than productive

The temptation is to stay busy, to manage the medications and the appointments and the logistics, because busyness keeps the grief at bay. But what the dying need most is not your efficiency. It is your presence. Sit with them. Hold the hand. Be there when nothing needs to be done, when there is only the quiet and the breathing. Some of the most sacred hours of your life will be the ones where you accomplished nothing and simply stayed. Productivity is how we hide from death. Presence is how we honor the person dying.

## Let them talk about dying if they want to

Many people protect their dying loved ones from the subject of death, steering every conversation toward false cheer, and in doing so they leave the dying person alone with the one thing they most need to talk about. If they want to speak of dying, let them. Let them say their fears. Let them give instructions, make peace, say goodbye. Do not rush in with "don't talk like that, you're going to be fine." That sentence, meant as comfort, slams a door they were trying to open. Be brave enough to sit in the truth with them.

## Help them finish what needs finishing

The dying often have business to complete, and helping them complete it is a profound gift. The words that need saying, "I love you," "I forgive you," "forgive me," "thank you," "goodbye." The relationships that need mending. The faith questions that need a pastor. Make space for these. Bring the estranged child to the bedside. Call the minister. Help them say the things, because the unsaid things become the heaviest part of the grief that follows. Let them leave nothing essential unspoken.

## Tend the body with dignity

Dying is physical, and the care is often intimate and humbling, the feeding, the cleaning, the turning. Do it gently and without making them feel like a burden. The body that is failing carried this person through their whole life and still houses someone made in the image of God. Touch them with tenderness. Speak to them even when they cannot answer, because hearing is among the last senses to go. Dignity at the end is one of the last and best gifts you can give.

## Care for yourself, because this is a marathon

Caregiver collapse is real and common, and you cannot care for the dying from an empty tank. Accept help. Let others sit the shift so you can sleep. Eat. Step outside. Find someone to talk to about your own grief, which is real and which you are not permitted to suppress just because you are the strong one. Running yourself to ruin does not honor your loved one. Staying whole enough to keep loving them does.

## Entrust them to God at the threshold

There comes a point where the only thing left to do is to release them, to give permission to go, to commend them into the hands that made them. "Into your hands I commit my spirit," Jesus said from the cross, and you can pray those words over the one you love. The Christian does not hand a loved one into nothing. The resurrection means the door they are walking through opens onto something, onto Someone, and you let them go not into the dark but into the keeping of God.

**This week:** If you are caring for someone now, do one thing to make space for what is unspoken, ask them gently if there is anyone they want to see, anything they need to say, any fear they are carrying alone. And do one thing to sustain yourself, ask a specific person to take one shift this week so you can rest. Both are part of the same love.

To walk someone to the threshold of death is to spend yourself almost completely, and you will come out of it grieving and hollowed and changed. You will also have done one of the truest things a human being can do, loved someone all the way to the end and not looked away. That is not a small thing. In the economy of God, it may be one of the largest.
